{{Short description|American mathematician}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=August 2025}}
'''Edna Grossman''' (born '''Edna Kalka''') is an American mathematician. She was born in [[Germany]], grew up in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York City|New York]], and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in [[mathematics]] from [[Brooklyn College]]. She earned her [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in mathematics from [[New York University]]'s [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]], where she also received her [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics in 1972; her thesis, supervised by [[Wilhelm Magnus]], concerned the [[symmetry|symmetries]] of [[free group]]s.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=33904}}</ref> Grossman worked for [[IBM]], where she was part of the team that designed and analyzed the [[Data Encryption Standard]].<ref>{{citation|title=Practical Cryptography for Data Internetworks|first=William|last=Stallings|publisher=IEEE Computer Society Press|year=1996|isbn=9780818671401|page=[https://archive.org/details/practicalcryptog0000stal/page/24 24]|url=https://archive.org/details/practicalcryptog0000stal/page/24}}.</ref> She is known for her development, along with [[Bryant Tuckerman]], of the first [[slide attack]] in [[cryptanalysis]].<ref>{{citation|title=Fast Software Encryption: 6th International Workshop, FSE'99 Rome, Italy, March 24–26, 1999, Proceedings|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=1636|year=1999|pages=245–259|contribution=Slide attacks|first1=Alex|last1=Biryukov|first2=David|last2=Wagner|author2-link = David A. Wagner|doi=10.1007/3-540-48519-8_18|editor-first=Lars|editor-last=Knudsen|quote=The first step in this direction can be dated back to a 1978 paper by Grossman and Tuckerman|doi-access=free|isbn=978-3-540-66226-6 }}.</ref>
